You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You implement one program task in the workspace you are given, against its own test suite, and you stop when the tests pass.

The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

5: /** Deterministic 32-bit PRNG so generated command sequences replay identically. */
6: function mulberry32(seed) {
7:   let a = seed >>> 0;
8:   return function next() {
9:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
10:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
11:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
12:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
13:   };
14: }

goal.objective:
Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. `src/index.js` must export `parsePointer`, `formatPointer`, `resolve`, `applyPatch` and the error classes `PointerError` and `PatchError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parsePointer(pointer)` turns pointer text into decoded reference tokens: the empty string is no tokens, and any other pointer must start with `/` and is split on every following `/`, so `'/'` is one empty token and `'//'` is two. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. The operations are `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`. `add` creates or overwrites an object member, and inside an array it inserts before the given index, where the index may equal the length and the token `-` appends. `remove` and `replace` require an existing target, and `replace` on the empty pointer replaces the whole document while `remove` on it throws `cannot remove the whole document`. `move` removes the value at `from` and adds it at `path`, is a no-op when the two pointers are equal, and throws `cannot move a value into its own child` when `from` is a proper prefix of `path`. `copy` adds an independent copy of the value at `from`. `test` compares the value at `path` with `value` as JSON — object members in any order, array elements in order, and no type coercion — and throws `test failed at /a/y` when they differ.

Every failure from `applyPatch` is a `PatchError` whose `index` is the 0-based position of the operation that failed; when the cause was a pointer failure, the message is that failure's message and `cause` is the `PointerError`. Operations are checked before they run: a non-object operation throws `operation must be an object`, an unrecognised or missing `op` throws `unknown operation: frob`, and missing members throw `add requires a path`, `add requires a value` or `move requires a from`. A patch that is not an array throws `patch must be an array`, and data that is not JSON throws `document is not JSON data` or `value is not JSON data`. Keys that shadow `Object.prototype`, including `__proto__`, are ordinary own properties throughout: adding `/__proto__` must leave the result's prototype and every other object alone, and resolving `/toString` on an empty object must fail. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

`src/index.js` must export `parsePointer`, `formatPointer`, `resolve`, `applyPatch` and the error classes `PointerError` and `PatchError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parsePointer(pointer)` turns pointer text into decoded reference tokens: the empty string is no tokens, and any other pointer must start with `/` and is split on every following `/`, so `'/'` is one empty token and `'//'` is two. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. The operations are `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`. `add` creates or overwrites an object member, and inside an array it inserts before the given index, where the index may equal the length and the token `-` appends. `remove` and `replace` require an existing target, and `replace` on the empty pointer replaces the whole document while `remove` on it throws `cannot remove the whole document`. `move` removes the value at `from` and adds it at `path`, is a no-op when the two pointers are equal, and throws `cannot move a value into its own child` when `from` is a proper prefix of `path`. `copy` adds an independent copy of the value at `from`. `test` compares the value at `path` with `value` as JSON — object members in any order, array elements in order, and no type coercion — and throws `test failed at /a/y` when they differ.

Every failure from `applyPatch` is a `PatchError` whose `index` is the 0-based position of the operation that failed; when the cause was a pointer failure, the message is that failure's message and `cause` is the `PointerError`. Operations are checked before they run: a non-object operation throws `operation must be an object`, an unrecognised or missing `op` throws `unknown operation: frob`, and missing members throw `add requires a path`, `add requires a value` or `move requires a from`. A patch that is not an array throws `patch must be an array`, and data that is not JSON throws `document is not JSON data` or `value is not JSON data`. 6: /**
7:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
8:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
10:  */
11: function mulberry32(seed) {
12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };
19: }

21: /**
22:  * Compares two strings by Unicode code point.
23:  * @param {string} a First string.
24:  * @param {string} b Second string.
25:  * @returns {number} Negative, zero, or positive.
26:  */
27: function byCodePoint(a, b) {
28:   const left = [...a];
29:   const right = [...b];
30:   for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(left.length, right.length); i += 1) {
31:     const diff = left[i].codePointAt(0) - right[i].codePointAt(0);
32:     if (diff !== 0) return diff;
33:   }
34:   return left.length - right.length;
35: }

39:  * @param {Iterable<string>} words Stored words.
40:  * @returns {Set<string>} Distinct prefixes.
41:  */
42: function prefixesOf(words) {
43:   const out = new Set(['']);
44:   for (const word of words) {
45:     const chars = [...word];
46:     for (let i = 1; i <= chars.length; i += 1) out.add(chars.slice(0, i).join(''));
47:   }
48:   return out;
49: }

1. First walking/creating the path without incrementing counts.
2. Only incrementing `count` on every node along the path when the word is genuinely new (`isNew`).
3. Setting `isWord = true` only in that new-word branch, and always updating `value`.

This ensures `count` (used for `size` and `countPrefix`) reflects only distinct stored words, correctly handling repeated inserts/updates.

- Real trie structure walked by Unicode code point (via `Array.from(str)`, which splits on code points, not UTF-16 code units)

- `countPrefix` in O(prefix length) via per-node counts
- `search` with optional `limit`, `entries()`, `longestPrefixMatch`
- Empty string treated as an ordinary word

goal.objective:
Finish `src/trie.js`, whose `Trie` class currently keeps words in a plain map. Build a real trie: one node per distinct prefix, walked by Unicode code point so a character outside the basic plane is a single step and never a pair of surrogate halves. Every listing is ordered by code point, so `'\uFF10'` comes before `'\uFFFD'` and both come before an emoji. You may add files under `src/`.

`insert(word, value)` stores a value and returns the value it replaced, or `undefined` when the word is new. `get(word)` and `has(word)` read it back. `delete(word)` removes a word, returns whether it removed one, and drops the nodes that word alone kept alive; deleting a string that is only a prefix of stored words removes nothing and returns `false`. `countPrefix(prefix)` returns how many stored words start with the prefix, and must cost the length of the prefix rather than a walk of the subtree, so keep a per-node count of the words below it. `search(prefix, limit)` lists the matching words in order, at most `limit` of them, defaulting to no limit; a prefix that is not in the index yields an empty list. `entries()` lists every `[word, value]` pair in order. `longestPrefixMatch(text)` returns `{ word, value }` for the longest stored word that is a prefix of `text`, or `null` when no stored word is.

The empty string is an ordinary word: it can be stored, it is a prefix of every string, and `countPrefix('')` is the number of stored words. `size` is the number of stored words. `nodeCount` counts nodes including the root, so an empty index has a node count of 1 and, after any sequence of inserts and deletes, the count equals the number of distinct prefixes of the stored words plus that root.

Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. goal.objective:
Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. Finish `src/heap.js` and `src/dijkstra.js`. `IndexedHeap` is a binary min-heap that also keeps an index from key to position, so `push`, `pop`, `remove`, `decreaseKey`, and `setPriority` each run in O(log n) while `has`, `peek`, and `priorityOf` are O(1). The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Errors are specific. A heap key that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string`; a priority that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `priority must be a finite number`; pushing a key that is already held raises `Error` with message `duplicate key: "a"`; re-prioritising a key that is not held raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown key: "a"`; and a `decreaseKey` that would raise a priority raises `RangeError` with message `priority must not increase for "a"`. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`; a node whose successors are not such an object raises `TypeError` with message `edge map for node "a" must be an object`; an edge or endpoint naming an undeclared node raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "q"`; a weight that is not a positive finite number raises `RangeError` with message `weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"`; and a non-string source raises `TypeError` with message `source must be a string`. 14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;

18:   };

9: /**
10:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
11:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
12:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
13:  */
14: function mulberry32(seed) {
15:   let a = seed >>> 0;
16:   return () => {
17:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
18:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
19:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
20:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
21:   };
22: }

24: /**
25:  * Computes distances with Bellman-Ford as an independent model.
26:  * @param {Record<string, Record<string, number>>} graph Weighted graph.
27:  * @param {string} source Start node.
28:  * @returns {Record<string, number>} Distance per node.
29:  */
30: function bellmanFord(graph, source) {
31:   const nodes = Object.keys(graph);
32:   const dist = {};
33:   for (const node of nodes) dist[node] = FAR;
34:   dist[source] = 0;
35:   for (let round = 0; round < nodes.length; round += 1) {
36:     for (const node of nodes) {
37:       if (dist[node] === FAR) continue;
38:       for (const [target, weight] of Object.entries(graph[node])) {
39:         if (dist[node] + weight < dist[target]) dist[target] = dist[node] + weight;
40:       }
41:     }
42:   }
43:   return dist;
44: }

The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). goal.objective:
Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. The operations are `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`. `add` creates or overwrites an object member, and inside an array it inserts before the given index, where the index may equal the length and the token `-` appends. `remove` and `replace` require an existing target, and `replace` on the empty pointer replaces the whole document while `remove` on it throws `cannot remove the whole document`. `move` removes the value at `from` and adds it at `path`, is a no-op when the two pointers are equal, and throws `cannot move a value into its own child` when `from` is a proper prefix of `path`. `copy` adds an independent copy of the value at `from`. `test` compares the value at `path` with `value` as JSON — object members in any order, array elements in order, and no type coercion — and throws `test failed at /a/y` when they differ.

Every failure from `applyPatch` is a `PatchError` whose `index` is the 0-based position of the operation that failed; when the cause was a pointer failure, the message is that failure's message and `cause` is the `PointerError`. A patch that is not an array throws `patch must be an array`, and data that is not JSON throws `document is not JSON data` or `value is not JSON data`. 33:  * @returns {string} the decoded token

35: function decodeToken(raw) {
36:   let result = '';
37:   for (let i = 0; i < raw.length; i += 1) {
38:     const char = raw[i];
39:     if (char === '~') {
40:       const next = raw[i + 1];
41:       if (next === '0') {
42:         result += '~';

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `tokenize`, `parse`, `evaluate` and the error class `ExprError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `tokenize(input)` returns tokens in source order, each `{ type, value, index }` where `index` is the 0-based position in UTF-16 code units. Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. Evaluation reports `division by zero at 1` for `/` or `%` with a zero divisor, and `non-finite result at 5` whenever an operation or call produces something that is not a finite number, each pointing at the operator or the call's name.

`evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. The callable functions are fixed: `abs`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties toward positive infinity), `sign` take exactly one argument; `pow` and `atan2` take exactly two; `min` and `max` take one or more. Calling anything else throws `unknown function: foo at 0`, and a wrong count throws `function abs expects 1 argument, got 2 at 0`, `function pow expects 2 arguments, got 1 at 0` or `function max expects at least 1 argument, got 0 at 0`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. Finish `src/heap.js` and `src/dijkstra.js`. `IndexedHeap` is a binary min-heap that also keeps an index from key to position, so `push`, `pop`, `remove`, `decreaseKey`, and `setPriority` each run in O(log n) while `has`, `peek`, and `priorityOf` are O(1). The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Errors are specific. A heap key that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string`; a priority that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `priority must be a finite number`; pushing a key that is already held raises `Error` with message `duplicate key: "a"`; re-prioritising a key that is not held raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown key: "a"`; and a `decreaseKey` that would raise a priority raises `RangeError` with message `priority must not increase for "a"`. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`; a node whose successors are not such an object raises `TypeError` with message `edge map for node "a" must be an object`; an edge or endpoint naming an undeclared node raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "q"`; a weight that is not a positive finite number raises `RangeError` with message `weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"`; and a non-string source raises `TypeError` with message `source must be a string`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

6: /**
7:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
8:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
10:  */
11: function mulberry32(seed) {
12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };
19: }

21: test('an empty heap reports nothing', () => {
22:   const heap = new IndexedHeap();
23:   assert.deepEqual([heap.size, heap.peek(), heap.pop(), heap.drain()], [0, undefined, undefined, []]);
24:   assert.deepEqual([heap.has('nope'), heap.priorityOf('nope'), heap.remove('nope')], [false, undefined, false]);
25: });

18:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
19:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;

goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. content.text:
`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. A token that is not a safe integer in `0 .. unions performed` raises `RangeError` with message `unknown checkpoint: 5`, quoting the token.

`src/kruskal.js` exports two functions over edges written `[u, v, weight]`. `minimumSpanningForest(count, edges)` takes the edges in weight order, breaking ties by first endpoint and then second endpoint, keeps an edge when it joins two different sets, and returns `{ edges, weight, components }` with the chosen edges in the order they were taken, their total weight, and how many components remain. `componentsWithAlternatives(count, baseEdges, alternatives)` applies the base edges once, then measures each alternative edge list on top of that base independently, rolling back between them, and returns `{ base, alternatives }` where `base` is the component count after the base edges and `alternatives` holds one component count per alternative.

Validate up front. A count that is not a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `count must be a non-negative integer`. An element that is not a safe integer in `0 .. count - 1` raises `RangeError` with message `element out of range: 7`, quoting the offending value. An edge list that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `edges must be an array`, an edge that is not a three-element array raises `TypeError` with message `edge must be [u, v, weight]`, a weight that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `weight must be a finite number`, and an alternatives argument that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `alternatives must be an array`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Summary of the implementation:

**`src/dsu.js`** — Added:
- Validation in the constructor (`count` must be a non-negative safe integer) and an `#checkElement` helper enforcing element bounds, used by `find`.
- No path compression in `find` (kept as a plain walk-to-root), so the union history stays perfectly invertible.
- Union-by-size: on each successful `union`, push `{ attached, root }` onto a private `#history` stack (the root that got attached beneath the other, and the surviving root).
- `checkpoint()` returns `this.#history.length` (the union count so far).
- `undo()` pops the last history entry, restores the attached subtree as its own root, subtracts its size back off the surviving root, bumps `#components`, and returns `true`/`false`.
- `rollback(token)` validates the token is a safe integer in `[0, history.length]` (else `RangeError: unknown checkpoint: <token>`), then calls `undo()` repeatedly until the history length matches, returning the count of undos performed.

**`src/kruskal.js`** — Added:
- Shared validators (`checkElement`, `checkEdges`) enforcing the `count`/element/edge/weight error messages, plus an `alternatives must be an array` check.
- `minimumSpanningForest`: sorts a copy of the edges by weight, then first endpoint, then second endpoint; runs them through a `DisjointSets`, keeping edges whose `union` succeeds; returns `{ edges, weight, components }`.
- `componentsWithAlternatives`: applies `baseEdges` once, takes a `checkpoint()`, then for each alternative list applies it, records `components`, and `rollback`s to the checkpoint before trying the next alternative — so alternatives are measured independently on top of the same base state.

goal.objective:
Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. A token that is not a safe integer in `0 .. unions performed` raises `RangeError` with message `unknown checkpoint: 5`, quoting the token.

`src/kruskal.js` exports two functions over edges written `[u, v, weight]`. `minimumSpanningForest(count, edges)` takes the edges in weight order, breaking ties by first endpoint and then second endpoint, keeps an edge when it joins two different sets, and returns `{ edges, weight, components }` with the chosen edges in the order they were taken, their total weight, and how many components remain. `componentsWithAlternatives(count, baseEdges, alternatives)` applies the base edges once, then measures each alternative edge list on top of that base independently, rolling back between them, and returns `{ base, alternatives }` where `base` is the component count after the base edges and `alternatives` holds one component count per alternative.

Validate up front. A count that is not a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `count must be a non-negative integer`. An element that is not a safe integer in `0 .. count - 1` raises `RangeError` with message `element out of range: 7`, quoting the offending value. An edge list that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `edges must be an array`, an edge that is not a three-element array raises `TypeError` with message `edge must be [u, v, weight]`, a weight that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `weight must be a finite number`, and an alternatives argument that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `alternatives must be an array`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. 4: import { Trie } from '../src/trie.js';

6: /**
7:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
8:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
10:  */
11: function mulberry32(seed) {
12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };
19: }
20: 
21: /**
22:  * Compares two strings by Unicode code point.
23:  * @param {string} a First string.
24:  * @param {string} b Second string.
25:  * @returns {number} Negative, zero, or positive.
26:  */
27: function byCodePoint(a, b) {
28:   const left = [...a];
29:   const right = [...b];
30:   for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(left.length, right.length); i += 1) {
31:     const diff = left[i].codePointAt(0) - right[i].codePointAt(0);
32:     if (diff !== 0) return diff;
33:   }
34:   return left.length - right.length;
35: }
36: 
37: /**
38:  * Every distinct prefix of a set of words, the empty prefix included.
39:  * @param {Iterable<string>} words Stored words.
40:  * @returns {Set<string>} Distinct prefixes.
41:  */
42: function prefixesOf(words) {
43:   const out = new Set(['']);
44:   for (const word of words) {
45:     const chars = [...word];
46:     for (let i = 1; i <= chars.length; i += 1) out.add(chars.slice(0, i).join(''));
47:   }
48:   return out;
49: }

goal.objective:
Finish `src/trie.js`, whose `Trie` class currently keeps words in a plain map. Build a real trie: one node per distinct prefix, walked by Unicode code point so a character outside the basic plane is a single step and never a pair of surrogate halves. Every listing is ordered by code point, so `'\uFF10'` comes before `'\uFFFD'` and both come before an emoji. You may add files under `src/`.

`insert(word, value)` stores a value and returns the value it replaced, or `undefined` when the word is new. `get(word)` and `has(word)` read it back. `delete(word)` removes a word, returns whether it removed one, and drops the nodes that word alone kept alive; deleting a string that is only a prefix of stored words removes nothing and returns `false`. `countPrefix(prefix)` returns how many stored words start with the prefix, and must cost the length of the prefix rather than a walk of the subtree, so keep a per-node count of the words below it. `search(prefix, limit)` lists the matching words in order, at most `limit` of them, defaulting to no limit; a prefix that is not in the index yields an empty list. `entries()` lists every `[word, value]` pair in order. `longestPrefixMatch(text)` returns `{ word, value }` for the longest stored word that is a prefix of `text`, or `null` when no stored word is.

The empty string is an ordinary word: it can be stored, it is a prefix of every string, and `countPrefix('')` is the number of stored words. `size` is the number of stored words. `nodeCount` counts nodes including the root, so an empty index has a node count of 1 and, after any sequence of inserts and deletes, the count equals the number of distinct prefixes of the stored words plus that root.

A limit that is neither `Infinity` nor a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `limit must be a non-negative integer`.
